Diffusion

/dih-FYOO-zhun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Diffusion means the process of spreading out gradually and widely — whether a substance, an idea, or a custom.

Linguists mapped the diffusion of the slang term from two coastal cities into classrooms across the country.

Worked Example

The journal's open-access policy accelerated the diffusion of the vaccine findings, which reached rural clinics within weeks instead of years.

The research did not stay locked in one place — it spread gradually outward until it reached a wide audience. Diffusion names that spreading process, not the research itself.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dispersal: Dispersal means scattering in different directions, the way a crowd breaks up or wind spreads seeds — the emphasis is on a cluster breaking apart, not on anything reaching a particular destination. Diffusion is also a spreading, but it tracks how far and how widely something travels until it is present everywhere it reaches.

spread: Spread is the everyday umbrella word for anything extending over a wider area — butter, rumors, wildfires. Diffusion is the more precise, analytical term for the gradual process by which something travels outward until it is widely present, and it is the word science and scholarship reach for.

dissemination: Dissemination is deliberate wide distribution, especially of information — there is a sender pushing the message out, the way a ministry disseminates guidelines. Diffusion has no sender: the thing drifts and spreads on its own, like a custom crossing borders over generations. Planned campaign, dissemination; unplanned drift, diffusion.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

concentration: gathering densely into one place

containment: keeping something within limits

Where it sits · how much ground it comes to cover — circulation → diffusion → saturation

circulation vs. diffusion: Circulation is milder than diffusion: a memo circulates within a single office, while diffusion carries something far beyond where it started.

saturation vs. diffusion: Saturation is stronger than diffusion: when a trend has diffused so completely that it is everywhere at once, we say the culture is saturated with it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dif-

Prefix — dif-: apart, in every direction (a form of dis-)

Root — fus

Root — fus: to pour (Latin fundere, fusus)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: act or process of

Put it together

Put it together: From Latin diffundere: dif- (apart, in every direction) + fundere (to pour) + -ion (act of) — something poured out in all directions until it spreads far from its source.

Use the root in a new word: infusion

Use the root in a new word: infusion: The café's new owner gave the menu an infusion of Oaxacan flavors, pouring fresh life into old recipes.

Word Choice

Academic / scientific

Diffusion emphasizes a gradual, largely unplanned spreading outward — perfume drifting through a room, a custom crossing borders over generations. Its cousin dissemination implies a deliberate sender: a ministry disseminates guidelines. If someone is actively pushing the message, dissemination is the more precise word; if it drifts and spreads on its own, use diffusion.
